interactions: Enzalutamide is a strong CYP3A4 inducer and a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 inducer: it lowers exposure to co-administered substrates; check any new drug against it.
Lactulose or rifaximin with enzalutamide, leuprolide, spironolactone or furosemide: no clinically relevant interaction (rifaximin is minimally absorbed).
Spironolactone and furosemide during lactulose titration: diarrhea and volume loss add to the risk of hypokalemia, hyponatremia and kidney injury; monitor electrolytes and creatinine.

output.summary: No clinically relevant interaction between lactulose or rifaximin and the current medicines. Enzalutamide is a strong CYP3A4 inducer, can lower the seizure threshold and can cause fatigue and cognitive impairment. Penicillin anaphylaxis: avoid beta-lactams without allergy advice. warnings: Enzalutamide: seizures reported in about 0.5% of patients; use caution with drugs that lower the seizure threshold. Fatigue, cognitive impairment, falls and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome are labeled adverse effects.
Enzalutamide in hepatic impairment: no starting-dose adjustment for Child-Pugh A to C; the half-life is prolonged in severe impairment.
Avoid benzodiazepines, opioids and sedating antihistamines in hepatic encephalopathy.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not give a penicillin or other beta-lactam without allergy specialist advice: documented penicillin anaphylaxis; if an infection is found, choose a non-beta-lactam agent.
required_recommendations: Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.

Identify and treat the precipitant: no infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, electrolyte disturbance or sedative was found, so check lactulose adherence and stool frequency on the prophylactic 20 mL twice-daily dose, and continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily.

Review with oncology at 4-8 weeks: if cognition has not returned to baseline once HE is controlled and lactulose adherence is confirmed, reconsider the diagnosis and the contribution of enzalutamide (fatigue, cognitive impairment, falls); counsel him and his wife on monitoring cognition and falls (ACG 2026 key concept 8).

Discuss goals of care with him and his wife, with hepatology and oncology: decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 13) with recurrent HE and castration-resistant prostate cancer; active extrahepatic malignancy generally precludes liver transplant listing.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 13); ammonia mildly elevated (64 µmol/L); enzalutamide CNS effects a potential secondary contributor; leptomeningeal carcinomatosis excluded by MRI.

differential.key_features: Enzalutamide causes fatigue, cognitive impairment, falls and rarely seizures or PRES; MRI shows no PRES and the asterixis and EEG slowing point to HE, but a contribution cannot be excluded until cognition is reassessed once HE is controlled.
Contrast MRI shows no leptomeningeal, dural or parenchymal enhancement and no calvarial metastasis; rare in prostate cancer.
Leuprolide-induced testosterone suppression contributes to cognitive/fatigue symptoms but not asterixis.
A 3-week course with asterixis and diffuse EEG slowing favors a metabolic encephalopathy; reassess cognition once HE is controlled.
Calcium 8.6 mg/dL (about 9.6 mg/dL corrected for albumin 2.7) excludes hypercalcemia.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh B (9: bilirubin 1.9 1, albumin 2.7 3, INR 1.5 1, mild ascites 2, HE grade II 2); MELD-Na 13 (creatinine 1.0, bilirubin 1.9, INR 1.5, sodium 138).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.

Androgen-receptor inhibitors that cross the blood-brain barrier (enzalutamide, apalutamide) can cause fatigue, cognitive impairment and falls; consider them when a patient with prostate cancer on these drugs presents with confusion.
Covert HE is minimal HE or West Haven grade 1; overt HE is grade 2 or higher (ACG 2026 key concept 1). Disorientation to time with asterixis is therefore overt HE, whatever the ammonia level.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Contrast MRI is appropriate to exclude metastatic and leptomeningeal disease, but the dominant treatable cause is HE; do not delay lactulose while awaiting the MRI.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue brain metastasis or leptomeningeal disease workup ahead of HE evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A mildly raised ammonia does not grade HE; the grade is clinical (West Haven grade II, overt).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C. is a 61-year-old man with NASH cirrhosis and castration-resistant prostate cancer on enzalutamide who presents with 3 weeks of slowly progressive confusion, emotional blunting, and passivity. His wife noticed he was no longer engaged in conversation, was having difficulty following complex discussions, and seemed 'far away.' He had a prior grade 1 HE episode 4 months ago that resolved with rifaximin; he has since taken rifaximin and lactulose 20 mL twice daily. He has had no fever, vomiting, melena, falls or new medicines.

neurological_exam.additional: No jaundice. Mild ascites on exam. Spiders absent. Wife notes he is passively apathetic, 'not himself' for 3 weeks.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, reactive. Extraocular movements intact. No nystagmus. Facial symmetry intact.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Oriented to person and place; disoriented to time. Slow processing. Mild asterixis. Wife notes behavioral change including passivity and emotional blunting over 3 weeks, possibly new compared with the prior episode.
